uncited: This method maps a 2D semantic label image to an RGB color image by assigning predefined colors to known classes and generating deterministic, high-contrast colors for unknown or unseen classes using a fixed HSV-to-RGB conversion.
It ensures visual consistency and distinctness for arbitrary label IDs without requiring user-defined palettes for every possible class.

It differs from [Categorical Color Maps](7160-categorical-color-maps.md) by using a deterministic hash-based hue generation for unknown labels rather than a fixed or random palette, and from [Style Transfer Function (1D)](777-style-transfer-function-1d.md) by operating on discrete integer labels rather than continuous scalar values.
Initialize `color_img` as an array of shape $(H, W, 3)$ with dtype `uint8`, typically zero-initialized.
Create a boolean mask $M_k$ where $M_k[i, j] = (\text{label\_img}[i, j] == k)$.
Assign the RGB tuple $\mathbf{c}_k = \text{_LABEL_COLORS}[k]$ to all pixels where $M_k$ is true.
Compute the set of unique IDs present in `label_img`: $U = \{\text{unique}(\text{label\_img})\}$.
Compute the set of known IDs: $K = \{\text{keys}(\text{_LABEL_COLORS})\}$.
Identify unseen IDs: $U_{unknown} = U \setminus K$.
Normalize hue to range $[0, 6)$: $h = h_{deg} / 60.0$.
Compute intermediate value: $x = c \times (1 - |h \pmod 2 - 1|)$.
Assign $(r, g, b)$ to all pixels where $\text{label\_img}[i, j] == uid$.
*   **Time Complexity:** $O(N)$ where $N = H \times W$, as each pixel is visited a constant number of times (once for known, once for unknown).
*   **Memory Complexity:** $O(N)$ for the output image.
*   **Strengths:** Deterministic output for any input label ID; no need to pre-define colors for all possible classes; high contrast between unknown classes due to HSV distribution.

*   **Limitations:** Unknown classes may have similar hues if IDs are close and the hash function does not spread them well (though 47 is a prime, aiding distribution); fixed saturation/value may not suit all visualization contexts.
*   **When to use:** When rendering semantic segmentations with a dynamic or unknown set of classes, or when a consistent, non-random mapping is required for reproducibility.
It addresses the need for robust visualization of semantic labels where the set of classes is not fixed or known in advance.
